title: Feedback must come back
author: Rod J. Naquin
summary: Rod J. Naquin, a high school ELA teacher who previously worked in education reform, argues that schools collect feedback but rarely respond to it. He recalls a project manager who analysed responses after each session and put participants' own words on the next day's slides, a practice he now follows with daily exit tickets. Drawing on Hannah Arendt's idea of "frozen thoughts," he suggests that phrases such as "we've always done it this way" excuse people from thinking, and that honest feedback can thaw them. He connects this to early research on toxic positivity at work, which describes pressure to suppress negative feelings and to insist things will improve, and warns that surveys become loyalty tests when only positive input is welcome. Gallup and Great Place To Work research is cited to show that asking without acting can hurt engagement. He ends with a four-move talk routine, "You said, so we'll, not yet because, I'll check back," for closing the loop out loud.
points: Naquin's central claim is that a feedback culture is measured not by how many surveys go out but by whether people see a response they recognise.
Arendt's "frozen thoughts" explain why stock school phrases like "buy-in" and "we've always done it this way" can answer a concern before anyone has considered it.
Toxic positivity turns surveys into loyalty tests, and rewarding participation with treats rewards compliance instead of honesty.
Gallup and Great Place To Work advise analysing results within days, choosing two or three priorities and being honest about what cannot change.
The "You said / So we'll / Not yet, because / I'll check back" routine gives teachers and leaders a concrete way to close the loop, with "Not yet, because" building the most trust.
quotes: The result is a place that barely responds: there’s no timely way to raise a concern and no sign that anyone heard it. I don’t blame any one person for this. It’s a matter of structure.
When a teacher raises a concern and hears “we’ve always done it this way,” the phrase has answered for everyone before anyone has actually thought about the concern.
Collecting it is safe. Responding means letting a long-standing habit be questioned in public.
If only positive feedback is welcome, a survey turns into a loyalty test. People figure that out quickly and either say what’s expected or skip it.
Research on workplace feedback keeps reaching the same conclusion: asking without acting can be worse than not asking at all.
Gallup recommends analyzing results within days or weeks and sharing them “while employees are still watching,” and an end-of-year survey misses that window.
A feedback culture isn’t measured by how many surveys go out. It’s measured by whether people can speak honestly and whether they see a response they recognize.
People skip “Not yet, because...” more than any of the other moves, and it does the most to build trust.
